content:
Apple is opposing a Justice Department request to overturn a court ruling that allowed the company to seek documents from more than a dozen federal agencies. Here's what's happening.

Some background

Weeks ago, Apple was granted permission to seek documents from 14 U.S. agencies as part of its defence against a Justice Department antitrust case filed in March 2024.

Those agencies and departments include:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Commerce Department
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Defense Department
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • State Department

Apple's argument is that if it can prove the federal government chose its products based on their privacy features, that evidence could support its claim that the practices the DOJ is challenging have legitimate justification rather than being anti-competitive.

After Apple's win in the dispute, the DOJ filed a motion asking Jose Linares, the retired federal judge serving as special master of discovery in the case, to reconsider his decision.

In complex cases involving large amounts of discovery, courts sometimes appoint special masters to handle narrower disputes to lighten the load on the presiding judge. Special masters can be retired judges, practising attorneys, or other experts with relevant experience.

In its motion, the DOJ asked the court to overturn Apple's discovery win on the grounds that Judge Linares applied the wrong legal standard by treating the agencies as parties to the case rather than third parties, who should receive greater protections in discovery.

The DOJ also said Apple's requests would impose undue burdens on the agencies, citing 13 newly submitted declarations in support, while claiming the documents are of limited importance because federal agencies are not "ordinary consumers."

"The motion is untenable in every respect"

Apple's response to the DOJ motion is now public, and the company didn't hold back in systematically dismantling each of the DOJ's arguments for overturning the ruling.

Apple cited a number of prior cases in arguing that "the special master correctly applied the legal standard for party discovery against federal agencies," and systematically dismantled the DOJ's arguments regarding undue burden and importance.

Apple stated in its conclusion:

Under the schedule Judge Linares set on August 4, no further written arguments will be accepted, and it's up to him whether to stick with the original discovery order or grant the DOJ's request for reconsideration.
